title: Mental capacity, Gillick & Fraser
blurb: The Mental Capacity Act's five principles, how capacity is tested, best interests, and how children consent: Gillick competence versus the Fraser guidelines.
question: A 14-year-old attends with her grandmother for a filling. She clearly understands the dentist's explanation and wants to go ahead, but her grandmother keeps answering for her. Who can consent, and how should the team involve the young person?

teach.h: Capacity: can this person make this decision now?
teach.body: Valid consent needs capacity: the ability to make a particular decision at the time it needs to be made. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. Someone may be able to agree to a scale and polish but not to complex surgery, or may lack capacity while unwell or intoxicated and regain it later. In England and Wales, people aged 16 and over are covered by the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA). Children under 16 are assessed for Gillick competence. Scotland has separate law: the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000.

letters.sub: Unless it is shown that the person lacks it
Take all practicable steps to help them decide first
An unwise choice doesn't mean someone lacks capacity
Anything done for a person who lacks capacity must be in their best interests
Choose the option that limits their rights and freedom least

teach.caption: These come from section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

steps.label: Retain
steps.sub: Long enough to make the decision

steps.label: Communicate
steps.sub: By any means: speech, writing, signs, blinking

teach.caption: If the person can't do any one of these because of an impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain (such as dementia, a learning disability or a head injury), they lack capacity for that decision.

teach.body: The clinician makes the decision in the person's best interests. That means considering their past and present wishes, beliefs and values, and consulting carers and family about what the person would want. Relatives cannot consent on behalf of an adult unless they hold a registered Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare that covers the decision, or are a court-appointed deputy. Where someone has no one to speak for them and a serious decision is needed, an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA) may be involved.

items.label: Gillick competent child, or a person with parental responsibility
Presumed able to consent to treatment; the MCA applies
Adult: consents for themselves unless they lack capacity

teach.caption: Parental responsibility: the mother; a father married to the mother or (for births since 2003) named on the birth certificate; others by court order or adoption. Grandparents and step-parents don't have it automatically.
Gillick competence is a test of a child's capacity. The Fraser guidelines are a narrower checklist for giving contraceptive advice without parents knowing.

teach.body: A child under 16 who has 'sufficient maturity to understand what is involved' is Gillick competent and can consent to that treatment, even if parents disagree. There is no fixed age or checklist: it depends on the child and on how complex the decision is. Talk to the young person directly, not just the adult with them, and involve them in decisions. Encourage them to involve their family, but respect their confidentiality unless there is a safeguarding concern.

teach.text: Don't mix them up: Gillick competence decides whether a child under 16 can consent to treatment, including dental treatment. The Fraser guidelines apply only to contraception and sexual health advice.

items: Capacity is specific to the decision and the time; assume it unless shown otherwise.
MCA five principles: assume capacity, support, unwise is allowed, best interests, least restrictive.
Test: understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate.
Relatives can't consent for an adult without a health and welfare LPA or deputyship.
Under 16: Gillick competence or someone with parental responsibility. 16 to 17: presumed able to consent.

summary: You can now apply the Mental Capacity Act's five principles and the four-part capacity test, explain best interests and who may decide for an adult, set out how consent works at different ages, and tell Gillick competence apart from the Fraser guidelines.

A.q: An adult patient with capacity refuses a recommended extraction, which the team thinks is unwise. What follows?
options: The dentist decides in her best interests
She must be assessed for dementia
A.why: Under the MCA, an unwise decision doesn't mean a person lacks capacity. Explain the consequences, respect her choice and record it.

whyNot.0: Best interests decisions apply only when someone lacks capacity.
whyNot.2: Family can't overrule an adult who has capacity.
whyNot.3: Making an unwise choice is not, on its own, a reason to question capacity.

A.q: Which of these is one of the four parts of the functional test of capacity?
A.why: The person must be able to understand, retain, use or weigh the information, and communicate their decision.

whyNot.0: Reading isn't required; information can be given in other ways.
whyNot.1: A person with capacity can disagree with the dentist.
whyNot.3: The MCA applies from age 16; age isn't part of the functional test.

A.q: A parent answers for a competent 15-year-old throughout the appointment. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Ask the parent to wait outside
Postpone treatment until the child is 16
A.why: A Gillick competent young person should be spoken to directly and involved in decisions about their care.

whyNot.0: This excludes a young person who can take part in decisions.
whyNot.1: Sending the parent out isn't necessary; involve the child while the parent is there.
whyNot.2: Gillick competent children don't need to wait until 16.

B.q: A parent brings a child for treatment. What should be recognised about consent?
options: Only the child can ever consent for themselves
It depends on age, capacity and authority
B.why: Who can consent depends on the child's age, whether they are Gillick competent, and who has parental responsibility.

whyNot.0: Only someone with parental responsibility can consent for a child who isn't competent.
whyNot.1: A parent can consent for a child who isn't Gillick competent.
whyNot.3: Children's treatment needs valid consent like anyone else's.

B.q: Which MCA principle says you must try everything practicable to help a person decide before concluding they can't?
B.why: A person must not be treated as unable to decide unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success.

whyNot.0: Assuming capacity is the starting point, but this principle is about helping them decide.
whyNot.2: Best interests applies once someone has been found to lack capacity.
whyNot.3: Least restrictive is about choosing the option that limits freedom least.

B.q: A patient's daughter says she will sign consent for her father, who has dementia. When could she legally do so?
options: If she holds a health and welfare LPA
If she is his named next of kin
If she lives with him as his carer
If he says today that she can sign for him
B.why: A relative can consent for an adult who lacks capacity only with a registered Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare (or as a court-appointed deputy).

whyNot.1: Next of kin has no legal power to consent for another adult.
whyNot.2: Living together gives no legal authority.
whyNot.3: If he lacks capacity, he can't validly appoint her on the spot.

C.q: What do the Fraser guidelines apply to?
options: Adults who lack capacity to consent
C.why: Fraser guidelines are specific to giving contraceptive and sexual health advice to under 16s without parental knowledge.

whyNot.0: Dental treatment for under 16s relies on Gillick competence.
whyNot.2: Adults lacking capacity are covered by the Mental Capacity Act.
whyNot.3: 16 and 17-year-olds are presumed able to consent to treatment.

C.q: From what age does the Mental Capacity Act 2005 apply?
C.why: The MCA applies to people aged 16 and over.

whyNot.0: At 12, a child's ability to consent is judged by Gillick competence.
whyNot.1: At 14, Gillick competence applies, not the MCA.

C.q: A patient lacks capacity to consent to a filling. Who usually makes the decision?
options: The clinician, in their best interests
The receptionist who booked them in
Any relative who attends with them
Nobody, so no treatment is given
C.why: Unless there's a valid LPA or deputy, the clinician decides in the person's best interests, after consulting carers and family.

whyNot.1: Reception staff don't make clinical decisions.
whyNot.2: Relatives are consulted but can't consent without legal authority.
whyNot.3: Treatment can go ahead if it is in the person's best interests.

reteach.title: Capacity is like a key for one door
reteach.question: Imagine each decision is a different door. Does having the key to one door mean you have the key to all of them?

blocks.body: A person holds the key to a door if they can understand, remember, weigh up and communicate that particular decision. Someone with mild dementia may hold the key to 'Can we clean your teeth today?' but not to 'Shall we take out four teeth under sedation?'. A 13-year-old may hold the key to a check-up but not to orthodontic surgery. Always ask: this person, this decision, right now. And always start by assuming they hold the key.

children.label: Gillick competent?
children.sub: Yes: child consents. No: parent with PR

children.label: Has capacity?
children.sub: Yes: patient consents. No: best interests

blocks.text: 'She's made a silly decision, so she must lack capacity' is wrong. An unwise decision on its own never proves lack of capacity.

explain.body: Assume capacity; support the person to decide; allow unwise decisions; act in best interests if they lack capacity; choose the least restrictive option.

test.q: Which is NOT one of the Mental Capacity Act's five principles?
options: A person is assumed to have capacity
Next of kin decide if in doubt
test.why: There is no MCA principle giving next of kin the decision. Best interests decisions are made by the decision-maker, usually the clinician.

explain.body: Can the person understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate the decision? Failing any one, because of an impairment of mind or brain, means they lack capacity for that decision.

test.q: A patient understands the explanation but forgets it within seconds, every time. Which part of the test is not met?
test.why: They must be able to retain the information long enough to make the decision.

whyNot.1: They do understand it at the time.
whyNot.3: The problem is memory, not weighing up.

explain.body: Under 16: Gillick competent children consent for themselves; otherwise a person with parental responsibility consents. 16 and 17: presumed able to consent. Fraser is only for contraception.

test.q: A grandmother brings a 9-year-old for an extraction. The child is not Gillick competent. Who can consent?
options: The grandmother, as she brought the child
The child, with the grandmother present
The dentist, in the child's best interests
test.why: If the child isn't competent, consent comes from someone with parental responsibility. Grandparents don't have it automatically.

whyNot.0: Bringing a child doesn't give legal authority to consent.
whyNot.1: The child isn't competent for this decision.
whyNot.3: Outside an emergency, the dentist needs consent from someone with parental responsibility.
